title: Reselling Products
subtitle: Test demand, true cost and product safety before your spare room becomes an unpaid warehouse

blocks.text: Reselling can begin with one useful product and a sensible margin. It can also begin with 80 novelty mugs arriving at your door like a ceramic intervention. This course builds the first version.

A reseller buys or acquires products and sells them for more than the full cost of getting them ready for a customer. The work is not simply finding a low purchase price. It includes checking demand, authenticity, safety, condition, fees, packaging, delivery, returns and records. A profitable listing is a calculation—not a hopeful adjective.
Choose one narrow category first. Familiarity makes it easier to recognize normal prices, defects, counterfeits, recalls and slow-moving stock.

items.title: Select a product category and buyer.
Calculate profit after every unit cost.
Run a small test batch with a stop rule.
“Anything bought cheaply can be resold profitably.”
items.text: A bargain without demand is inventory wearing a party hat. Profit depends on what actually sells, how quickly it sells and what the full transaction costs.

sections.title: Start With Evidence, Not a Shopping Mood

blocks.text: A shopping mood buys inventory. Evidence buys a business.

items.title: DEFINE THE BUYER
items.text: Name the person, need and price range. A category such as tested entry-level kitchen appliances is easier to research than “things people might enjoy.”

items.title: STUDY COMPLETED DEMAND
items.text: Compare recent sold results where available, not only asking prices. Note typical condition, selling time, delivery method and seasonal changes.

items.title: VERIFY THE SOURCE
items.text: Keep purchase records and check brands, model numbers, packaging and serial information. If authenticity is doubtful, do not advertise the item as genuine.

items.title: CHECK SAFETY
items.text: Search Health Canada recalls and current product requirements. Used products are still consumer products; a recalled or dangerous item does not become safe because it has a charming vintage description.

blocks.text: Health Canada’s consumer-product rules can apply to used goods. Never sell a recalled product unless the corrective action has been completed and resale is permitted.
Counterfeit goods can create legal, safety and refund problems. A low price and a heroic story about a cousin’s warehouse are not proof of authenticity.

items.title: “If another seller lists it for $100, mine is worth $100.”
items.text: A listing shows an invitation, not a completed sale. Compare actual sold evidence, condition and time-to-sale before choosing a price.

blocks.text: Health Canada: Industry guide to second-hand products

sections.title: Find the Profit Hidden Behind the Price Tag

blocks.text: Estimate unit profit by starting with the expected selling price, then subtract purchase cost, platform and payment fees, cleaning or repair, packaging, shipping or delivery, advertising and a reasonable allowance for returns or losses.
Revenue is the money received; profit is what remains after costs. Your bank balance may look enthusiastic before fees, inventory and tax have had their turn.
Inventory records support cost-of-goods-sold calculations. Track the item, purchase date, source, cost, sale date, selling price and related expenses.

items.title: “Small online sales do not need to be reported.”
items.text: CRA says income earned from peer-to-peer sales must be reported. Use Form T2125 for self-employment business income and keep supporting records.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: A repeatable resale business begins only after demand, legitimacy, safety and full unit economics are verified. Test small, record actual results and reorder from evidence—not excitement.

paragraphs: Priya Desai saw insulated tumblers listed for $38 and bought 30 at $19 each. By Tuesday, the boxes had formed a small municipal council in her hallway. Her spreadsheet, unfortunately, had only two columns: “cost” and “future riches.”

The conflict appeared after her first sales. Payment fees, packaging and delivery reduced the margin; two lids leaked; and the $38 competitors were mostly asking prices, not sold prices. Priya also lacked clear supplier documents for the brand claim.

She paused the listings, refunded the affected customers and verified the product source and safety. For her next category, she bought six unbranded desk organizers, calculated every cost, set a 30-day stop rule and recorded actual selling time. Four sold at the target margin, so she reordered ten—not 100.
Priya did not abandon reselling. She replaced warehouse optimism with a controlled experiment, and her hallway returned to civilian government.

blocks.text: A test batch answers three questions cheaply: will it sell, at what true profit and with what problems? Reordering is earned by results.
A hopeful bulk order became a disciplined test batch once the real costs and sold evidence were checked.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why should a reseller study sold results instead of asking prices?
items.detail: A listing price is only an invitation to buy; sold results show what buyers actually paid, in what condition and how quickly.

items.title: Which costs belong in a true unit-profit calculation?
items.detail: Purchase cost, platform and payment fees, cleaning or repair, packaging, shipping or delivery, advertising and a reasonable allowance for returns or losses.

items.title: What should happen before a used product is offered for sale?
items.detail: Its safety, recall status and authenticity should be checked—a recalled or dangerous item is not safe simply because it looks vintage.

items.title: Why does a small test batch reduce risk?
items.detail: It answers whether the product will sell, at what true profit and with what problems, before committing to a larger order.

items.title: When can GST/HST registration become required?
items.detail: Generally after taxable supplies exceed $30,000 in one calendar quarter or across four consecutive calendar quarters.

items.title: Cost of goods sold
items.text: Inventory cost connected with products sold during the period.

items.title: Unit profit
items.text: Expected sale price minus all costs attached to one item.

items.title: Sell-through
items.text: Share of available inventory sold during a period.

items.title: Test batch
items.text: Small first order used to measure real demand and problems.

items.title: Recall
items.text: Official action concerning a product with a safety issue.

items.title: Counterfeit
items.text: Unauthorized imitation presented as a genuine product.
